title: Public Spirit 9, 2026
author: Chrys Dougherty
source: The Active Citizen's Guide to Improving Schools (chrysdougherty.substack.com), November
summary: Chrys Dougherty closes his five-part series on educating informed citizens with a post on public spirit. His central claim is that caring about the common good is not enough: a curriculum must also give students the background knowledge to think productively about the issues they care about. He lists the knowledge areas a public-spirited citizen needs, namely evidence-based reasoning, cognitive biases, human nature, liberal democracy and economics. He then adds dispositions such as open-mindedness, cooperation for mutual benefit, positive-sum thinking and a broad common identity. The post ties civic formation to a knowledge-rich curriculum that starts in kindergarten rather than high school. It ends with two books on school civics programs that make the same point about gaps in background knowledge.
points: Public-spiritedness programs that only raise awareness and caring fall short because students lack the knowledge to reason about the problems.
Evidence-based reasoning depends on subject knowledge, which is why Dougherty argues for a broad, knowledge-rich curriculum.
Students should be taught cognitive biases such as confirmation bias and myside bias, which affect even PhD-level academics.
Understanding human nature, including tribalism, status competition and cumulative knowledge, helps explain cruelty toward out-groups and the need for institutional protections.
Dispositions like positive-sum thinking and cooperation for mutual benefit, illustrated by the PTA, are teachable parts of civic education.
quotes: Efforts to promote public-spiritedness often focus on making students aware of problems and encouraging them to care. But caring alone is not enough. The curriculum must also help students develop the background knowledge they need to think productively about the issues they care about.
This is why students need a knowledge-rich curriculum that gives them broad subject-area knowledge.

Students should be aware of confirmation bias, the tendency to notice favorable evidence for one’s beliefs and ignore contradictory evidence. The group version of confirmation bias is “myside bias,” near-automatic rejection of ideas that contradict your group’s preferred beliefs.
A third feature is humans’ cooperative ability to create knowledge that is passed down but that any single individual would have difficulty re-creating from scratch.

Aspiring change agents need to learn how to understand and work with people with whom they disagree, distinguishing disagreements over facts from differences in values. They should understand the difference between persuading people and “winning” arguments, keeping in mind that persuading people usually involves finding common ground.

Parents don’t walk into a PTA meeting announcing that they are mainly interested in the education of their own children, though that is exactly why they are there. Instead, they emphasize working together to benefit all of the students in the school in the understanding that this will benefit their own children.
A major theme in both books is that gaps in students’ background knowledge are a major impediment to their ability to think well about local or national issues.
